title: ExVerus: Verus Proof Repair via Counterexample Reasoning
one_liner: Instead of guessing proofs once, ExVerus lets an LLM learn by seeing what breaks, then fixing it.
lead: Writing mathematical proofs is hard—even for programs. When an LLM tries to write a proof for code and the proof fails, it usually just gets retried without knowing WHY it failed. ExVerus changes this by showing the LLM concrete counterexamples (actual program traces that break the proof), then asking it to block those failures by writing rules that prevent them. It is not magic spell-checking; it is learning-from-mistakes the way a student improves by seeing their wrong answers.

paras: A proof is a program written in special code (Verus) that convinces a machine that some other program works correctly. For example, a proof might say: if you give my list-sorting function a 10-item list, it will always return a sorted list.

Until now, LLMs (language models) write proofs in one shot—read the code, guess the proof, hit enter. If it fails, they have only the error message, which is often cryptic. The LLM does not know: what trace of the program made the proof wrong? What actually happened when you ran the code? A beginner fixes homework by seeing test cases fail; an LLM fixing proofs sees only a wall of text saying proof rejected.

This is frustrating because the proof often nearly works. One condition is wrong, one invariant (a rule that must always be true) is missing, and the whole thing collapses. But the LLM does not know which piece to change.

callout.html: Show the LLM concrete program runs where the proof breaks, then ask it to patch the proof by writing rules that block those runs.

steps.text: Given code, the model generates Verus proof assertions (claims about what must be true).
The Verus machine checks if the proof is correct. If not, it halts.
ExVerus simulates the code and finds concrete data (a list, a number) that violates the proof.
The model sees the exact program run and why it fails, not an abstract error.
The model writes new invariants (guard rules) to exclude the broken case. Try again.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes how an LLM gets feedback when writing proofs. Instead of receiving only a yes/no from the verifier, it receives concrete examples of program behavior that break the proof—data values, execution traces, the actual reason the proof failed.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: what went wrong
hidden.name: proof counterexample
paras: A proof counterexample is not a complicated statistic—it is a concrete program trace: a specific list of numbers, a specific path through the code, specific variable values at a specific point. It is what went wrong, pinned down as data you can see.

The paper extracts this by running the code and checking which inputs cause the proof's claim to fail. It then feeds this concrete trace back to the LLM. Instead of guessing what went wrong from an error message, the LLM sees proof failure caused by real program behavior, and writes proof rules to exclude that behavior.

heat.caption: Darker means more helpful to learning. Concrete traces and guided repair are the core.

reads.html: When your proof fails, you need to know what your code actually did. A counterexample is that moment: the exact data and the exact point where your claim broke. The paper makes that visible to the LLM.

The paper's key technical move is generating counterexamples via bounded model checking and feeding them to the LLM to guide inductive invariant synthesis. Inductive invariants are loop-proof guards (rules that remain true in every iteration).

paras: Proof generation is a search problem. The LLM is trying to find invariants (rules) that make the proof succeed. Without feedback, it is searching blind—restarting from the same initial guess over and over. With concrete counterexamples, the search is guided: the LLM learns which invariants do not work and why, then proposes new ones that block the broken case. This is feedback-driven repair, not restart.

Counterexamples work because they unambiguously show what went wrong. Seeing that input [1, 5, 2] broke your loop invariant is way more useful than an abstract error about failed proof step 47. The LLM can then pattern-match: what property would have blocked [1, 5, 2]? And write a rule. This narrows the search space dramatically. Each failed proof generates new constraints; each constraint guides the next attempt closer to success.

stages.s: LLM writes invariants to block it

math.words: new invariant = old invariant OR (NOT condition that makes counterexample fail). Repeat until proof holds.
math.equation: I_new = I_old OR block_counterexample(c_1, c_2, ..., c_k)
symbols: a new logical condition that forbids the counterexample

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Old proof invariant: 'every element in the array is positive'.
Verifier found counterexample: array = [1, -3, 5]. This breaks the invariant.
LLM writes new invariant: 'every element in the array is positive, OR the array has length < 3'. This blocks the counterexample [1, -3, 5].
Repeat: new invariant is checked. If a new counterexample breaks it, LLM refines further.
After a few rounds, the invariant is strong enough that no counterexample breaks it—proof passes.

math.note: Each repair adds a new logical clause to block a seen failure. Over iterations, the invariant becomes precise enough to succeed.

bars.h2: How repair by counterexamples beats blind retries

charts.title: Old approach: LLM retrying without feedback
charts.note: No new information between attempts. Without knowing what failed, the LLM has no reason to nudge its guess in a productive direction—it is equally likely to move away from the solution as toward it.

charts.title: ExVerus: learning from counterexamples
rows: Attempt 2: blocks A, sees counterexample B
Attempt 3: blocks A and B, sees counterexample C
Attempt 4: blocks A, B, C—proof passes
charts.note: Each failure teaches something specific. Invariants grow precise, proof accuracy climbs, and tokens are used more wisely (fewer blind retries).

items.html: If the tool finding counterexamples is imperfect, it might miss broken cases. Then the invariant looks good locally but fails on untested data. The paper bounds the search (checks a finite set of inputs), so there is always a risk of missing edge cases.

The LLM might write invariants that block the seen counterexamples but are too narrow. Example: if one counterexample is the array [1, -3, 5], the LLM might write 'forbid arrays of length exactly 3' instead of 'forbid negative numbers'. The fix fails on a different length-3 array.
Some properties of loops are not learnable by an LLM in a reasonable time. If the true invariant is mathematically complex or subtle, the counterexample loop may not converge.
The LLM generalizes counterexamples (writes rules that block the counterexample class, not just the one case), and the loop terminates when the invariant is strong enough.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small Verus program (e.g. a list-reversal or array-search function) that needs a loop invariant. Write a version without the correct invariant on purpose. Run ExVerus: let it generate one counterexample, have the LLM write a patch, check if the patch blocks it. Repeat for 2-3 rounds, watching the invariant grow and the proof get closer to passing. Show token counts: ExVerus uses fewer tokens overall than a naive LLM retrying blindly, because each guess is guided.
demo.metric_eq: proof_success_rate = (number of proofs that pass) / (number of proofs attempted); token_efficiency = proof_success_rate / (total tokens used)
demo.closing: The key visual: after round 1 (counterexample shown), the next proof attempt is not a random restart—it directly addresses the failure. That is learning, not guessing.
